subtopic_detail: Native valve endocarditis empiric therapy
stem:
You are the medical registrar on call at a metropolitan hospital. A 54 year old woman presents with 3 weeks of fevers, malaise, and back pain. She has no injecting drug use and no recent dental procedures. She had rheumatic fever aged 12.

On examination she has a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge that was not previously documented, two small tender nodules on her finger pads, and splinter haemorrhages on two nail beds. There is no prosthetic material in situ. The team have taken three sets of peripheral blood cultures from three different sites over the past hour. Renal function and inflammatory markers are back within the last 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 128/72, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 38.4
data_table.Examination: New early diastolic murmur left sternal edge; two tender finger-pad nodules; splinter haemorrhages
data_table.Investigations: Blood cultures x3 taken and pending; CRP 118 mg/L; ESR 82 mm/h

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empiric antibiotic regimen to commence now?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin dosed by lean body weight
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin covers viridans streptococci but misses methicillin sensitive Staphylococcus aureus which now accounts for the largest share of native valve endocarditis in Australia; empiric cover before culture results must include an antistaphylococcal agent (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Intravenous ceftriaxone monotherapy at 2 g once daily for the initial 48 hours
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy misses MSSA at the doses used for streptococcal endocarditis and does not provide the synergistic gentamicin cover recommended while awaiting culture results (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin oral loading over the first 24 hours
options.rationale: The triple combination with rifampicin is reserved for prosthetic valve endocarditis which is not present here; adding rifampicin for native valve disease increases hepatotoxicity and drug interactions without added benefit (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Intravenous flucloxacillin plus benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin at reduced synergy dose
options.rationale: For subacute native valve endocarditis with no prosthetic material the recommended empiric therapy adds flucloxacillin for MSSA to benzylpenicillin for streptococci and low-dose gentamicin for synergy pending culture identification (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand IE Position Statement).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

options.text: Oral amoxicillin plus clavulanate pending transthoracic echocardiography and culture results
options.rationale: Oral therapy is not appropriate for empiric endocarditis; bactericidal intravenous therapy is standard until at least 2 weeks of parenteral treatment have completed and the patient meets specific oral switch criteria (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic

explanation.summary: Native valve subacute infective endocarditis without prosthetic material is empirically treated with intravenous benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus low-dose gentamicin per Therapeutic Guidelines. The regimen covers viridans streptococci, MSSA, and provides synergy pending speciation. Rifampicin is added only for prosthetic valve disease. Oral therapy is inadequate for initial management.
key_points: Empiric native valve IE: benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus low-dose gentamicin
Rifampicin only for prosthetic valve endocarditis
Blood cultures x3 from separate sites before antibiotics where clinically safe
MSSA is the most common causative organism in Australian native valve IE now
explanation.pearls: Gentamicin for endocarditis synergy is dosed 1 mg/kg every 8 hours (not the usual 5-7 mg/kg daily) and levels are monitored for renal toxicity beyond 2 weeks.

sources.label: Cardiac Society of Australia and New Zealand IE Position Statement

subtopic_detail: Osteoporosis pharmacotherapy selection with GORD
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar reviewing a 72 year old woman in the fracture clinic after a low trauma wrist fracture that occurred stepping off a kerb.

Her DEXA today shows lumbar spine T score -3.1 and femoral neck T score -2.6. She has known Barrett's oesophagus on annual surveillance and cannot tolerate lying flat after meals due to reflux breakthrough. Her creatinine clearance is 34 mL/min. She lives alone, drives independently, and has no dental problems. She has never been on antiresorptive therapy. Calcium and vitamin D are replete. She asks for the treatment that best suits her situation without triggering her reflux.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74, BP 132/78, RR 14, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: Kyphosis mild; no dental caries; healed wrist cast off
data_table.Investigations: DEXA lumbar T -3.1; femoral neck T -2.6; 25OH vitamin D 82 nmol/L; corrected calcium 2.32 mmol/L
data_table.Blood tests: Creatinine 138 micromol/L; eGFR 34 mL/min; PTH 4.8 pmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly taken with a full glass of water in the morning
options.rationale: Oral bisphosphonates are contraindicated in patients with active upper gastrointestinal disease including Barrett's oesophagus and are also relatively contraindicated by an eGFR below 35 mL/min; both problems apply here (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; Osteoporosis Australia Position Statement).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Intravenous zoledronic acid 5 mg annual infusion after paracetamol premedication
options.rationale: Zoledronic acid is contraindicated when creatinine clearance is below 35 mL/min because of the risk of acute kidney injury post infusion; her eGFR of 34 mL/min sits below this threshold (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg every six months with monitored calcium and vitamin D
options.rationale: Denosumab is renally safe below eGFR 35 mL/min, avoids the upper gastrointestinal issues that rule out oral bisphosphonates, and is first line for her severity of osteoporosis with a recent fragility fracture; hypocalcaemia risk is managed by ensuring vitamin D and calcium replete before dosing (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook; PBS denosumab restriction criteria).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook
PBS denosumab restriction criteria

options.text: Oral raloxifene 60 mg daily with counselling on venous thromboembolism risk
options.rationale: Raloxifene reduces vertebral but not hip fracture risk and is not first line for severe osteoporosis with recent non-vertebral fragility fracture where hip fracture prevention is a priority; it also raises VTE risk (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Subcutaneous teriparatide 20 mcg daily as the first-line antiosteoporotic agent
options.rationale: Teriparatide on the PBS requires two prior minimal trauma fractures with a T score below -3 despite antiresorptive therapy for at least 12 months, so it is not first-line before antiresorptive treatment (Source: PBS teriparatide restriction criteria).
source_refs: PBS teriparatide restriction criteria

explanation.summary: Selection of osteoporosis therapy must integrate renal function, upper GI comorbidity, and PBS access criteria. Barrett's oesophagus and eGFR under 35 mL/min both rule out oral and intravenous bisphosphonates. Denosumab suits both problems and covers hip fracture prevention. Teriparatide on the PBS is reserved for failure of antiresorptive therapy plus severe disease.
key_points: Zoledronic acid contraindicated when CrCl below 35 mL/min
Oral bisphosphonates contraindicated in Barrett's oesophagus
Denosumab safe across renal function, dosed six-monthly
Ensure calcium and vitamin D replete before denosumab to prevent hypocalcaemia
explanation.pearls: Missing a denosumab dose beyond 7 months provokes rebound vertebral fractures; use of denosumab must be continuous or transitioned to a bisphosphonate on cessation.

subtopic_detail: Acute ischaemic stroke thrombolysis eligibility
stem:
You are the neurology registrar reviewing a 68 year old man in the emergency department at 06:45.

He was last known well at 21:00 the previous evening when he went to bed. His wife noted right sided weakness and inability to speak when she woke at 06:00 today. CT brain plain and CT perfusion have just been completed; the plain scan shows no established infarct or haemorrhage and CT perfusion shows a mismatch of 42 mL ischaemic core with 118 mL penumbra in a left middle cerebral artery distribution. He weighs 82 kg. His usual medications include perindopril and metformin. No recent surgery, no anticoagulants. Blood pressure has settled at 168/92 after topical GTN.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88 regular, BP 168/92, RR 16, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.9
data_table.Examination: Right facial droop; expressive dysphasia; right hemiparesis MRC 2/5
data_table.Investigations: CT brain plain unremarkable; CT perfusion core 42 mL, penumbra 118 mL, mismatch ratio 2.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in acute reperfusion therapy?

options.text: Withhold reperfusion therapy because the last known well time exceeds nine hours from symptom detection
options.rationale: The last known well time is what determines the window, not symptom detection; wake up stroke can still be treated if perfusion imaging shows a favourable core to penumbra mismatch under current AU stroke pathway (Source: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Administer intravenous tenecteplase now, then refer for endovascular thrombectomy assessment
options.rationale: The EXTEND and WAKE UP trial paradigm supports tenecteplase or alteplase for unknown onset stroke with perfusion mismatch up to 9 hours from midpoint of sleep, and this patient has a substantial salvageable penumbra with a favourable ratio; concurrent large vessel occlusion is assessed for thrombectomy in parallel (Source: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Proceed directly to endovascular thrombectomy without administering intravenous thrombolysis first
options.rationale: Standard AU practice is to give intravenous thrombolysis where eligible and proceed to thrombectomy in parallel unless there is a contraindication; skipping thrombolysis when eligible has not been shown non-inferior in the Australian setting (Source: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Commence dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and clopidogrel for secondary prevention
options.rationale: Dual antiplatelet therapy is used for minor ischaemic stroke or high risk TIA where reperfusion is not indicated; it is contraindicated within 24 hours of thrombolysis and is not the acute reperfusion decision here (Source: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines

options.text: Give intravenous labetalol to lower blood pressure below 140/90 before any reperfusion decision
options.rationale: Aggressive lowering below 140/90 is not required before thrombolysis; the pre thrombolysis target is under 185/110 which has already been achieved with topical GTN in this case (Source: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines).
source_refs: Stroke Foundation Clinical Guidelines

explanation.summary: Wake up stroke with favourable perfusion mismatch is treatable with intravenous thrombolysis under the extended window criteria supported by EXTEND. Tenecteplase is now first-line at many Australian centres. Thrombectomy is assessed in parallel for large vessel occlusion. Pre thrombolysis blood pressure target is under 185/110.
key_points: Wake up stroke may still be thrombolysed if perfusion mismatch favourable
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg bolus is now standard at many Australian centres
Pre thrombolysis BP target under 185/110
Thrombectomy is not withheld by giving IV thrombolysis first
explanation.pearls: The core to penumbra mismatch ratio required for extended window treatment is at least 1.8 with an ischaemic core under 70 mL per the EXTEND trial protocol.

subtopic_detail: Cushings syndrome first-line screening choice
stem:
You are the endocrinology registrar. A 44 year old woman is referred by her GP with new central weight gain of 12 kg over 8 months, easy bruising, and difficult to control hypertension despite three agents. She has a violaceous striae distribution over her flanks.

She works rotating night shifts as an ICU nurse, sleeps 3 to 4 hours in fragmented blocks during the day, and drinks two to three standard drinks a night. Menstrual cycle is regular. She takes no exogenous steroids, no inhaled corticosteroids, and no complementary medicines. Random morning cortisol at 07:00 is elevated. Diabetes screen is normal. She asks about the best first screening test that will not be confounded by her circumstances.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 168/104 on 3 agents, RR 14, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: Central adiposity; supraclavicular fat pads; violaceous striae flanks; proximal weakness
data_table.Investigations: 07:00 cortisol elevated; HbA1c 5.6%; K 3.5

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line screening test for Cushing's syndrome in this patient?

options.text: Late night salivary cortisol collected on two separate consecutive nights at bedtime
options.rationale: Late night salivary cortisol requires a consistent day-night sleep pattern to interpret because its diagnostic threshold assumes physiological nadir during actual sleep; rotating shift work with fragmented daytime sleep invalidates the reference range (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushings 2008).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushings 2008

options.text: Inferior petrosal sinus sampling with sequential ACTH gradients bilaterally in one sitting
options.rationale: Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is an invasive tertiary test to localise ACTH source after screening confirms Cushings and cross sectional imaging is equivocal; it is never a first-line investigation (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushings 2008).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushings 2008

options.text: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test with a morning cortisol at 08:00 the next day
options.rationale: The overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test relies on a stable circadian rhythm to interpret the morning cortisol; shift work disrupts baseline diurnal secretion and increases false positive rates (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushings 2008).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushings 2008

options.text: Corticotropin releasing hormone stimulation testing with sequential cortisol measurements
options.rationale: CRH stimulation is used to differentiate between pituitary and ectopic ACTH sources after biochemical Cushings has been established; it is not a first-line screening test for Cushings syndrome (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushings 2008).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushings 2008

options.text: 24 hour urinary free cortisol measurement performed twice, each collection from separate days
options.rationale: 24 hour urinary free cortisol is validated as a first-line screen and is not affected by shift work sleep patterns because it measures total daily production over an integrated 24 hour window; two collections improve sensitivity (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushings 2008).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushings 2008

explanation.summary: First-line Cushing's syndrome screening tests include late night salivary cortisol, overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression, and 24 hour urinary free cortisol. Shift work invalidates the two circadian rhythm dependent tests, so 24 hour urinary free cortisol on two separate days is the best choice here. Confirmatory and localising tests come after biochemical diagnosis.
key_points: 24 hour urinary free cortisol integrates production and bypasses circadian confounding
Late night salivary cortisol assumes stable nocturnal sleep
Overnight dexamethasone suppression assumes stable diurnal rhythm
Two elevated screening results are required before proceeding to localisation
explanation.pearls: Late night salivary cortisol has 92% sensitivity for Cushings only when the patient reliably sleeps overnight; shift work drops sensitivity below 60% and demands the urinary alternative.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Cushings 2008

subtopic_detail: Acute pericarditis first-line management
stem:
You are the medical registrar assessing a 32 year old man in the emergency department with pleuritic central chest pain of 4 days duration.

The pain is worse when lying flat and improves when sitting forward. He had a coryzal illness 10 days ago. There is a friction rub at the lower left sternal edge. Troponin is negative on serial testing at 3 and 6 hours. Echocardiography shows no wall motion abnormalities, ejection fraction 62%, and a trivial pericardial effusion. ECG shows widespread saddle shaped ST elevation with PR depression. He has no history of tuberculosis exposure, no known malignancy, and no immunosuppression.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 88, BP 122/74, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 37.4
data_table.Examination: Friction rub lower left sternal edge; no elevated JVP; no pulsus paradoxus
data_table.Investigations: ECG widespread saddle ST elevation with PR depression; troponin negative x2; TTE trivial effusion, EF 62%
data_table.Blood tests: CRP 84 mg/L; creatinine 76 micromol/L; eGFR over 90

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line treatment regimen for this presentation?

options.text: Empiric intravenous piperacillin plus tazobactam pending pericardial fluid culture confirmation
options.rationale: Bacterial pericarditis presents with high fever, sepsis, and purulent effusion; the clinical picture and negative markers here point to viral or idiopathic cause and empiric broad spectrum antibiotics are not indicated (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guidelines on Pericardial Disease 2015).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guidelines on Pericardial Disease 2015

options.text: Oral prednisolone 25 mg daily tapered over four weeks as monotherapy for symptom control
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy is associated with a higher recurrence rate and is reserved for aspirin or NSAID contraindication or specific autoimmune cause; first-line remains NSAID plus colchicine (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guidelines on Pericardial Disease 2015).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guidelines on Pericardial Disease 2015

options.text: Urgent pericardiocentesis to obtain fluid for cytology and microbiological workup
options.rationale: Pericardiocentesis is indicated for tamponade or when malignant or bacterial cause is suspected; a trivial effusion without haemodynamic compromise in an otherwise well young man does not warrant this (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guidelines on Pericardial Disease 2015).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guidelines on Pericardial Disease 2015

options.text: Oral ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily plus oral colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily for three months
options.rationale: Standard first-line treatment for acute idiopathic pericarditis in a low risk adult is a nonsteroidal agent for symptom control combined with colchicine for at least 3 months to reduce recurrence rates by roughly 50 per cent per the COPE and ICAP trials (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guidelines on Pericardial Disease 2015; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guidelines on Pericardial Disease 2015
Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular

options.text: Loading dose oral aspirin 300 mg followed by dual antiplatelet therapy for six weeks minimum
options.rationale: Dual antiplatelet therapy addresses acute coronary syndrome, not pericarditis; the widespread ST changes with PR depression, negative troponin, and normal wall motion argue against ischaemia and pericardial anticoagulation raises bleeding risk (Source: European Society of Cardiology Guidelines on Pericardial Disease 2015).
source_refs: European Society of Cardiology Guidelines on Pericardial Disease 2015

explanation.summary: Acute idiopathic pericarditis in a low risk adult is treated first-line with a nonsteroidal agent plus colchicine for at least three months. Colchicine halves the recurrence rate compared with NSAID alone. Steroids are second-line for NSAID intolerance or specific autoimmune cause. Trivial effusions do not require drainage.
key_points: First line: NSAID plus colchicine for at least 3 months
Colchicine 0.5 mg twice daily for 3 months (COPE and ICAP trials)
Steroids reserved for NSAID intolerance or autoimmune cause
Drainage only for tamponade or suspected purulent or malignant effusion
explanation.pearls: PR segment depression on ECG is a specific marker for pericarditis with roughly 80 per cent specificity, distinguishing it from early repolarisation which shows PR isoelectric.

sources.label: European Society of Cardiology Guidelines on Pericardial Disease 2015

subtopic_detail: Steroid stress dosing during acute illness
stem:
You are the medical registrar admitting a 58 year old woman with community acquired pneumonia and a systolic blood pressure of 88 mmHg despite two litres of intravenous crystalloid.

She was diagnosed with primary adrenal insufficiency four years ago after a bilateral adrenalectomy for macronodular hyperplasia and takes hydrocortisone 15 mg on waking, 5 mg at lunch, and 5 mg at 5 pm plus fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily. She has taken her morning hydrocortisone dose this morning and doubled her dose at home yesterday when the fever started. She has an emergency medic-alert bracelet. Her blood glucose is 3.6 mmol/L and sodium is 132. She looks unwell and mottled.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 88/54, RR 26, SpO2 92% room air, temperature 39.2
data_table.Examination: Mottled peripheries; capillary refill 4 seconds; adrenalectomy scars
data_table.Investigations: CXR right middle lobe consolidation; lactate 3.8 mmol/L; glucose 3.6

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate steroid intervention?

options.text: Continue her usual oral hydrocortisone regimen and reassess response after antibiotics
options.rationale: Oral cortisol absorption is unreliable in septic shock; a patient with primary adrenal insufficiency and shock needs parenteral cortisol replacement immediately to prevent adrenal crisis (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency 2016).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency 2016

options.text: Give intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg over the following 24 hours by infusion
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis in known primary adrenal insufficiency during septic shock is treated with an immediate 100 mg intravenous hydrocortisone bolus followed by 200 mg per 24 hours as an infusion or divided doses; the infusion also covers mineralocorticoid needs at these doses (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency 2016).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency 2016

options.text: Administer intramuscular dexamethasone 8 mg then commence oral prednisolone twice daily
options.rationale: Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and cannot substitute for hydrocortisone in primary adrenal insufficiency crisis; it is only useful when biochemical testing of the pituitary axis is planned and hydrocortisone would interfere (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency 2016).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency 2016

options.text: Triple her oral hydrocortisone total daily dose split into six oral doses over the coming day
options.rationale: Even tripled sick-day oral doses are inadequate for adrenal crisis with shock and are absorbed too unreliably; parenteral therapy is required and oral dosing resumes when the patient can eat and is haemodynamically stable (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency 2016).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency 2016

options.text: Increase her fludrocortisone to 200 mcg oral daily and continue oral hydrocortisone unchanged
options.rationale: In doses over 40 mg per day of hydrocortisone the mineralocorticoid activity of hydrocortisone itself is sufficient and separate fludrocortisone escalation adds no benefit; the immediate priority is parenteral glucocorticoid rather than oral fludrocortisone adjustment (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency 2016).
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency 2016

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis in primary adrenal insufficiency requires immediate parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg per 24 hours as infusion. Oral absorption is unreliable in shock. Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and is reserved for testing. Fluid resuscitation, treatment of the precipitant, and glucose correction run in parallel.
key_points: Bolus hydrocortisone 100 mg IV then 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion
Hydrocortisone above 40 mg per day covers mineralocorticoid requirement
Oral dosing is inadequate in shock
Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid effect
explanation.pearls: The 'sick day rule' for outpatients is double the maintenance dose for febrile illness and triple for major surgery; a shocked crisis needs intravenous therapy regardless.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency 2016

subtopic_detail: Newly diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis DMARD selection
stem:
You are the rheumatology registrar. A 42 year old woman presents with 4 months of symmetrical polyarthritis affecting the MCPs, PIPs, and wrists.

She has morning stiffness of 90 minutes duration and swelling of at least six small joints. Rheumatoid factor is 148 IU/mL and anti-CCP is 210 U/mL. CRP is 42 mg/L and ESR is 62 mm/h. She has one child aged 4 and is not planning further pregnancies. She has no history of liver disease, no alcohol excess, and no evidence of latent tuberculosis on QuantiFERON. Her baseline eye examination and pulmonary function are within normal limits. She asks about the standard first-line agent.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 122/78, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Symmetric MCP and PIP swelling; wrist synovitis; no nodules
data_table.Investigations: Rheumatoid factor 148 IU/mL; anti-CCP 210 U/mL; CRP 42 mg/L; ESR 62 mm/h
data_table.Blood tests: Creatinine 68 micromol/L; ALT 22; hepatitis serology negative; QFT negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line DMARD to commence now?

options.text: Oral methotrexate 10 mg once weekly with folic acid 5 mg on the following day
options.rationale: Methotrexate is the anchor conventional synthetic DMARD for newly diagnosed seropositive rheumatoid arthritis; it is started at 10 to 15 mg weekly with folic acid on the day after each dose and titrated up to 25 mg over 8 to 12 weeks (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Subcutaneous adalimumab 40 mg every two weeks after latent TB screening
options.rationale: Biologic DMARDs including TNF inhibitors are reserved on the PBS for patients who have failed adequate trials of at least two conventional synthetic DMARDs; adalimumab is not first-line (Source: PBS biologic DMARD restriction; Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).
source_refs: PBS biologic DMARD restriction

options.text: Oral hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice daily as monotherapy indefinitely with retinal screening
options.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine is only appropriate as monotherapy for very mild seronegative disease; her seropositive polyarthritis with elevated inflammatory markers requires methotrexate as first-line (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology

options.text: Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily monotherapy as ongoing background disease control indefinitely
options.rationale: Corticosteroid monotherapy is not adequate maintenance for rheumatoid arthritis; it can be used as bridging therapy while DMARD onset occurs but must be tapered off (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology

options.text: Oral sulfasalazine 1 g twice daily monotherapy with regular full blood count monitoring
options.rationale: Sulfasalazine is used when methotrexate is contraindicated or in triple therapy combination; it is not the preferred initial single-agent DMARD for seropositive rheumatoid arthritis (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology).
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Rheumatology

explanation.summary: Methotrexate is the first-line conventional synthetic DMARD for newly diagnosed rheumatoid arthritis. It is started weekly at 10 to 15 mg with folate cover and titrated to 25 mg over 8 to 12 weeks. Biologics are reserved for failure of two conventional DMARDs on the PBS. Steroids are bridging only.
key_points: Methotrexate is the anchor DMARD for RA
Folic acid 5 mg on day after methotrexate reduces toxicity
Biologics require failure of at least 2 conventional DMARDs on PBS
Prednisolone only as bridging while DMARDs take effect
explanation.pearls: Methotrexate reaches full effect at 8 to 12 weeks; interim symptom control uses prednisolone at 7.5 mg or intra-articular steroid rather than dose escalation of methotrexate.

subtopic_detail: SIADH vs cerebral salt wasting differentiation
stem:
You are the medical registrar reviewing a 61 year old woman on day 5 of admission after coiling of a ruptured anterior communicating artery aneurysm.

Her serum sodium has fallen from 138 to 122 mmol/L over 48 hours. She is drowsy but rousable and complains of thirst. Her fluid balance chart shows 4200 mL out and 3600 mL in over the last 24 hours, weight has decreased 1.4 kg since admission, mucous membranes are dry, and skin turgor is reduced. Urine sodium is 92 mmol/L and urine osmolality is 486 mOsm/kg. Serum osmolality is 254 mOsm/kg. Cortisol and thyroid function are within normal limits.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 106, BP 108/62 lying and 92/58 standing, RR 18, SpO2 97% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes; reduced skin turgor; postural drop 16 mmHg
data_table.Investigations: Urine sodium 92 mmol/L; urine osmolality 486 mOsm/kg; serum osmolality 254 mOsm/kg
data_table.Blood tests: Sodium 122; potassium 4.4; urea 8.2; cortisol 320 nmol/L; TSH 1.8

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management of her hyponatraemia?

options.text: Fluid restriction to 800 mL per day with strict monitoring of daily weights and sodium levels
options.rationale: Fluid restriction is the treatment for SIADH which requires euvolaemia; this patient is hypovolaemic with postural drop, weight loss, and negative fluid balance, so restricting fluid will worsen her cerebral perfusion and vasospasm risk (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Guidelines: Hyponatraemia in Neurologic Patients).
source_refs: Neurocritical Care Society Guidelines: Hyponatraemia in Neurologic Patients

options.text: Intravenous hypertonic 3 per cent saline 150 mL bolus over 20 minutes then 100 mL bolus repeated
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline bolus is indicated for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia with seizures or coma; this patient is drowsy but rousable without seizures, so cautious isotonic correction is preferred to avoid osmotic demyelination (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Guidelines: Hyponatraemia in Neurologic Patients).
source_refs: Neurocritical Care Society Guidelines: Hyponatraemia in Neurologic Patients

options.text: Continuous intravenous 0.9 per cent saline at 100 mL per hour with fludrocortisone 100 mcg oral daily
options.rationale: The clinical picture of dry mucous membranes, postural drop, weight loss, and high urine sodium after subarachnoid haemorrhage fits cerebral salt wasting rather than SIADH; volume replacement plus fludrocortisone to reduce natriuresis is the treatment (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Guidelines: Hyponatraemia in Neurologic Patients).
source_refs: Neurocritical Care Society Guidelines: Hyponatraemia in Neurologic Patients

options.text: Oral urea 30 g daily with encouraged free water intake to promote osmotic diuresis of solutes
options.rationale: Oral urea is used for chronic mild SIADH not tolerating fluid restriction; it worsens the volume depletion of cerebral salt wasting and encouraging free water intake compounds the hyponatraemia (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Guidelines: Hyponatraemia in Neurologic Patients).
source_refs: Neurocritical Care Society Guidelines: Hyponatraemia in Neurologic Patients

options.text: Tolvaptan 15 mg oral once daily with sodium correction rate limited to 8 mmol per 24 hours
options.rationale: Tolvaptan is a vaptan approved for SIADH that promotes free water excretion; in a hypovolaemic patient with cerebral salt wasting it would precipitate profound hypovolaemia and shock (Source: Neurocritical Care Society Guidelines: Hyponatraemia in Neurologic Patients).
source_refs: Neurocritical Care Society Guidelines: Hyponatraemia in Neurologic Patients

explanation.summary: Cerebral salt wasting after subarachnoid haemorrhage is distinguished from SIADH by volume status: CSW is hypovolaemic while SIADH is euvolaemic. Both have elevated urine sodium and low serum osmolality. Fludrocortisone plus isotonic saline treats CSW; fluid restriction treats SIADH. Getting this wrong risks vasospasm in CSW or worsening hyponatraemia in SIADH.
key_points: CSW is hypovolaemic; SIADH is euvolaemic
Both have high urine sodium and low serum osmolality
Fludrocortisone plus saline for CSW
Fluid restriction for SIADH; vaptan or urea if refractory
explanation.pearls: In post-subarachnoid haemorrhage patients, fluid restriction is contraindicated because it worsens delayed cerebral ischaemia from vasospasm even if SIADH is later confirmed.

sources.label: Neurocritical Care Society Guidelines: Hyponatraemia in Neurologic Patients
European Endocrine Journal Hyponatraemia Practice Guideline

subtopic_detail: Postpartum haemorrhage escalation after uterotonic
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar. A 33 year old G3P2 has had a spontaneous vaginal birth of a 4200 g infant 25 minutes ago after a 3 hour first stage augmented with syntocinon and a 45 minute second stage.

On delivery she received 10 units syntocinon intramuscularly. The uterus is boggy at the umbilicus and she has passed 1200 mL of fresh red blood after delivery of the placenta which appears complete. The team has begun uterine massage, has emptied her bladder with a catheter, and has established a second wide bore intravenous line. She has no known coagulopathy or hypertensive disorder of pregnancy. Her group and hold is valid. She is alert, cool at the periphery, and pale.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118, BP 96/54, RR 22, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.4
data_table.Examination: Boggy uterus at umbilicus; ongoing PV loss; complete placenta on inspection
data_table.Investigations: Estimated blood loss 1200 mL; group and hold valid; Hb baseline 118 g/L
data_table.Medications: 10 units syntocinon IM at delivery; two wide bore IVs sited

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic to administer given ongoing atonic haemorrhage?

options.text: Repeat intramuscular syntocinon 10 units into the deltoid muscle of the opposite arm
options.rationale: Once initial syntocinon fails, escalation to a syntocinon infusion plus a second-line agent is preferred; repeat bolus intramuscular syntocinon is not the RANZCOG escalation step (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Intramuscular ergometrine 250 mcg after confirming the patient has no hypertensive disorder
options.rationale: Ergometrine 250 mcg intramuscularly is the second-line uterotonic per RANZCOG when initial syntocinon has failed, provided the patient has no hypertensive disorder of pregnancy which is a contraindication; a syntocinon infusion is often set up in parallel (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Intramuscular carboprost 250 mcg with regular observation for bronchospasm at repeat doses
options.rationale: Carboprost is a third-line uterotonic used when syntocinon and ergometrine have failed; it is contraindicated in asthma and requires ergometrine to be trialled first per RANZCOG (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g bolus over 10 minutes as the primary uterotonic step now
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic adjunct used alongside uterotonics per the WOMAN trial and RANZCOG; it does not replace the uterotonic ladder because it does not address the atony that is the primary problem (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Sublingual misoprostol 800 mcg administered as tablets under the tongue as a single dose
options.rationale: Misoprostol is reserved for settings without access to injectable uterotonics or as adjunct fourth-line therapy per RANZCOG; it is not the second step when ergometrine is available and not contraindicated (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

explanation.summary: The RANZCOG PPH uterotonic ladder is syntocinon then ergometrine then carboprost then misoprostol. Ergometrine 250 mcg intramuscularly is second-line where hypertensive disorders are absent. Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic adjunct rather than a uterotonic. Non-pharmacological measures continue in parallel.
key_points: First-line syntocinon; second-line ergometrine
Ergometrine contraindicated in hypertensive disorders of pregnancy
Carboprost contraindicated in asthma
TXA is adjunct not uterotonic replacement
explanation.pearls: The uterotonic ladder progresses in 5 to 10 minute intervals; simultaneous major haemorrhage protocol activation and manual bimanual compression occur while the pharmacological ladder is being escalated.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 43 Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

subtopic_detail: Preeclampsia with severe features seizure prophylaxis
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 27 year old primigravida at 34+3 weeks who presented with a headache that has not settled with paracetamol.

Her booking BP was 108/64. Today her BP is 162/108 confirmed on two readings 20 minutes apart. She has right upper quadrant pain, brisk reflexes, and no clonus. Bloods: platelets 118, ALT 82 U/L, creatinine 84 micromol/L, urate 0.42 mmol/L. Urine dipstick is 3+ protein and PCR is 148 mg/mmol. Foetal CTG is reassuring and biometry from last week was on the 22nd centile with normal Dopplers. She has no seizure history. Betamethasone loading was given at 32 weeks for threatened preterm labour that settled.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92, BP 162/108, RR 16, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.6, FHR 138 with accelerations
data_table.Examination: Brisk reflexes; no clonus; RUQ tenderness; no epigastric mass
data_table.Investigations: Urine PCR 148 mg/mmol; urate 0.42 mmol/L; CTG reassuring

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological priority?

options.text: Oral labetalol 200 mg then titrate 200 mg every 4 hours while planning imminent birth
options.rationale: Oral labetalol is appropriate for mild to moderate pre-eclampsia but severe range hypertension needs faster onset therapy; parenteral or fast onset oral agents with tighter monitoring are required first (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023).
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023

options.text: Intravenous frusemide 40 mg to reduce blood pressure and address the mild renal impairment
options.rationale: Diuresis reduces intravascular volume which is already contracted in pre-eclampsia and impairs placental perfusion; frusemide is not indicated unless there is pulmonary oedema (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023).
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes then infusion at 1 g per hour
options.rationale: Severe pre-eclampsia with severe range BP plus symptoms of severe features such as headache and epigastric pain has a high risk of eclampsia; SOMANZ recommends magnesium sulfate loading and infusion for seizure prophylaxis in severe pre-eclampsia while blood pressure control and delivery planning occur (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023).
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023

options.text: Intravenous phenytoin 1 g loading over 20 minutes at 50 mg per minute for prophylaxis
options.rationale: The MAGPIE trial showed magnesium sulfate superior to phenytoin for eclampsia prophylaxis; phenytoin is no longer recommended for this indication (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023).
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023

options.text: Second dose of betamethasone 11.4 mg intramuscular now to complete lung maturation
options.rationale: A full course of betamethasone was already given at 32 weeks; repeat doses are not routinely indicated within 2 weeks and do not address the immediate maternal risk of eclampsia (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023; RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 24 Antenatal Corticosteroids).
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline 2023

explanation.summary: Severe pre-eclampsia with severe range hypertension plus symptomatic features requires magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis and parenteral antihypertensive therapy in parallel with birth planning. Loading dose 4 g over 20 minutes then infusion 1 g per hour per SOMANZ. Phenytoin is inferior. Diuretics not routinely used unless pulmonary oedema.
key_points: MgSO4 4 g loading then 1 g/h infusion for severe pre-eclampsia
Continues for 24 hours after birth or last seizure
Monitor reflexes, respiratory rate, urine output
Rescue dose 2 g bolus for seizure recurrence
explanation.pearls: Magnesium toxicity is monitored clinically; loss of patellar reflex is the earliest sign at 3.5 to 5 mmol/L, respiratory depression at 5 to 6.5 mmol/L, arrest above 12 mmol/L. Calcium gluconate 1 g IV is the antidote.

subtopic_detail: National Cervical Screening Program recall pathway
stem:
You are the GP registrar reviewing a 34 year old asymptomatic woman for her routine cervical screening test.

Her previous screening was 4 years ago and was HPV negative. She has had two sexual partners, is HPV vaccinated (three-dose schedule aged 14), and has no history of abnormal cytology. She has never had a colposcopy. She has no immunosuppression and has never been pregnant. Today's collected cervical screening test returns HPV oncogenic types other than 16 or 18 detected, with liquid based cytology showing low grade squamous intraepithelial lesion. There is no visible lesion on speculum examination and no post coital bleeding.

data_table.Examination: Cervix pink; no visible lesion; no contact bleeding
data_table.Investigations: HPV other oncogenic detected; LBC LSIL; endocervical cells present
data_table.History: Prior HPV negative 4 years ago; vaccinated adolescent series; no immunosuppression

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in her cervical screening pathway?

options.text: Refer for colposcopy within 8 weeks for direct visualisation of the transformation zone
options.rationale: Colposcopy is indicated for HPV 16 or 18 detected, or for HPV other oncogenic detected with high grade cytology; low grade cytology with HPV other in an immunocompetent woman is managed with a 12 month repeat test (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the Management of Screen-Detected Abnormalities 2020).
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the Management of Screen-Detected Abnormalities 2020

options.text: Repeat the HPV test in 12 months as intermediate risk follow-up with cytology reflex
options.rationale: HPV other oncogenic types with low grade cytology in an immunocompetent woman is intermediate risk under the NCSP; 12 month repeat HPV testing with reflex cytology is the guideline pathway; clearance at 12 months returns her to routine 5 year screening (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the Management of Screen-Detected Abnormalities 2020).
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the Management of Screen-Detected Abnormalities 2020

options.text: Return to routine 5 year screening because low grade findings do not require any interim step
options.rationale: Any oncogenic HPV detected on a screening test moves the patient off the 5 year routine schedule until the intermediate risk pathway clears; routine schedule return happens after 12 month HPV clearance (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the Management of Screen-Detected Abnormalities 2020).
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the Management of Screen-Detected Abnormalities 2020

options.text: Perform loop electrosurgical excision procedure on the transformation zone within 4 weeks
options.rationale: LEEP is a treatment for confirmed high grade dysplasia diagnosed at colposcopy, not a screening step; screening abnormalities never go directly to excision (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the Management of Screen-Detected Abnormalities 2020).
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the Management of Screen-Detected Abnormalities 2020

options.text: Repeat cytology alone in 6 months without repeating the HPV assay component this cycle
options.rationale: The Australian program uses primary HPV testing as the screening backbone; the 12 month follow-up test is HPV based with reflex cytology, not cytology alone (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the Management of Screen-Detected Abnormalities 2020).
source_refs: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the Management of Screen-Detected Abnormalities 2020

explanation.summary: The Australian National Cervical Screening Program uses primary HPV testing 5 yearly. HPV 16 or 18 detected requires colposcopy. HPV other oncogenic detected with negative or low grade cytology is intermediate risk and repeats HPV testing at 12 months with reflex cytology. HPV other with high grade cytology goes to colposcopy.
key_points: Primary HPV screening every 5 years for HPV negative results
HPV 16/18 detected: refer colposcopy
HPV other with LSIL or negative cytology: 12 month repeat HPV
HPV other with HSIL: refer colposcopy
explanation.pearls: Immunocompromised women follow a modified pathway with 3 year rather than 5 year routine screening intervals; this patient is immunocompetent.

sources.label: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines for the Management of Screen-Detected Abnormalities 2020
Cancer Council Australia Cervical Cancer Prevention

subtopic_detail: Ectopic pregnancy methotrexate vs surgical criteria
stem:
You are the gynaecology registrar assessing a 28 year old woman with a 4 week history of amenorrhoea and 2 days of right iliac fossa discomfort.

She is haemodynamically stable, has no significant pain, and describes only mild dull ache. Transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus with a 22 mm right adnexal mass with a yolk sac visible but no foetal cardiac activity; there is no free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum bhCG is 3800 IU/L. She has one previous term birth by uncomplicated vaginal delivery and no previous ectopic pregnancy. Her liver function, renal function, and full blood count are within normal limits. She lives 25 minutes from the hospital, has a reliable partner, and understands the need for weekly follow-up.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/74, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Soft abdomen; mild RIF tenderness; no rebound; cervical motion tenderness absent
data_table.Investigations: Empty uterus on TVUS; right adnexal 22 mm mass with yolk sac; no cardiac activity; no free fluid
data_table.Blood tests: bhCG 3800 IU/L; Hb 128; ALT 22; creatinine 68; blood group O positive

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line management?

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingectomy of the affected tube as first line surgical management
options.rationale: Surgical management is required per RANZCOG when bhCG is 5000 IU/L or above, when foetal cardiac activity is present, mass is 3.5 cm or larger, or the patient is haemodynamically compromised; this patient meets none of those and methotrexate is appropriate (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 24 Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 24 Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Mifepristone 200 mg oral followed by misoprostol 800 mcg sublingual as combined medical therapy
options.rationale: Mifepristone plus misoprostol is used for medical termination of intrauterine pregnancy; it is not effective for ectopic pregnancy trophoblast where methotrexate is the active agent (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 24 Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 24 Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Expectant management with bhCG trending downwards over 48 hours without intervention
options.rationale: Expectant management is limited to bhCG below 1500 IU/L that is falling on repeat testing and no adnexal mass beyond a small suspicious area; a 22 mm mass with visible yolk sac and bhCG 3800 IU/L exceeds these criteria (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 24 Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 24 Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Laparoscopic salpingostomy with linear incision on the tube and evacuation of trophoblast
options.rationale: Salpingostomy is a fertility preserving surgical option when the contralateral tube is diseased; it is not first line ahead of medical management when methotrexate criteria are met (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 24 Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 24 Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg per square metre body surface area with weekly bhCG monitoring
options.rationale: The RANZCOG methotrexate criteria are met: haemodynamically stable, minimal pain, bhCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no foetal cardiac activity, no significant haemorrhage, and reliable follow-up; single dose methotrexate 50 mg per square metre is the standard regimen (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 24 Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 24 Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

explanation.summary: The RANZCOG threshold for mandating surgical management of ectopic pregnancy is bhCG 5000 IU/L or above, foetal cardiac activity present, mass 3.5 cm or larger, significant pain, or haemodynamic instability. Below all these thresholds with reliable follow-up, single dose methotrexate 50 mg per square metre is preferred. Expectant needs bhCG under 1500 falling.
key_points: Surgery required if bhCG 5000+, FCA present, mass 3.5 cm+, pain, or unstable
Methotrexate: bhCG <5000, no FCA, mass <3.5 cm, stable, reliable follow-up
Expectant: bhCG <1500 and falling
Rh negative women need anti-D regardless of pathway
explanation.pearls: Methotrexate follow-up measures bhCG on day 4 and day 7 after dose; a fall of 15 per cent between day 4 and day 7 predicts success; failure of that fall prompts a second dose or surgery.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Gyn 24 Diagnosis and Management of Ectopic Pregnancy

subtopic_detail: Gestational diabetes OGTT interpretation Australian criteria
stem:
You are the antenatal clinic registrar reviewing a 32 year old woman at 27 weeks in her second pregnancy.

Her BMI at booking was 29. Her sister has type 2 diabetes. Her first pregnancy was uncomplicated. Today she brings the results of the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test performed 4 days ago at 26+3 weeks. Fasting plasma glucose was 5.2 mmol/L, 1 hour was 10.6 mmol/L, and 2 hour was 7.8 mmol/L. She is otherwise well, her BP is normal, and foetal biometry is on the 55th centile. She asks whether these numbers mean she has gestational diabetes and what the next step is.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6, FHR 140
data_table.Examination: Fundal height appropriate; foetal movements felt
data_table.Investigations: OGTT fasting 5.2 mmol/L; 1 hour 10.6 mmol/L; 2 hour 7.8 mmol/L; foetal biometry 55th centile
data_table.History: BMI 29 at booking; family history T2DM; previous uncomplicated pregnancy

lead_in: How should the OGTT result be interpreted and what is the appropriate management step?

options.text: GDM diagnosed on fasting alone; commence twice daily NPH insulin at 0.2 units per kilogram
options.rationale: Insulin is not routinely first-line before dietary intervention; also her fasting value 5.2 mmol/L exceeds the ADIPS threshold 5.1 mmol/L so the diagnosis is made but the immediate step is not insulin (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Gestational Diabetes 2014).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Gestational Diabetes 2014

options.text: Commence metformin 500 mg twice daily immediately as monotherapy without lifestyle intervention
options.rationale: Metformin can be used in GDM but ADIPS pathway begins with dietary intervention and home monitoring; pharmacotherapy is added if glucose targets are not met after 1 to 2 weeks of lifestyle intervention (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Gestational Diabetes 2014).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Gestational Diabetes 2014

options.text: OGTT is within normal limits at this gestation; no follow-up test or intervention required now
options.rationale: The fasting value 5.2 mmol/L is above the ADIPS threshold 5.1 mmol/L for diagnosing GDM; the diagnosis cannot be dismissed as normal (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Gestational Diabetes 2014).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Gestational Diabetes 2014

options.text: Repeat the OGTT at 32 weeks because a single elevation is insufficient to confirm the diagnosis
options.rationale: A single 75 g OGTT with any one elevated value confirms GDM per ADIPS; no repeat testing is needed for diagnosis (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Gestational Diabetes 2014).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Gestational Diabetes 2014

options.text: GDM diagnosed on fasting and 1 hour; refer for structured dietary and blood glucose monitoring
options.rationale: ADIPS criteria for GDM diagnosis after 75 g OGTT are any one of fasting 5.1 mmol/L or above, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or above, or 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or above; her fasting 5.2 and 1 hour 10.6 both exceed thresholds so GDM is confirmed and first-line management is diabetes educator plus dietitian plus 4 point home glucose monitoring (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Gestational Diabetes 2014).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Gestational Diabetes 2014

explanation.summary: ADIPS 75 g OGTT thresholds diagnose GDM if any one is met: fasting 5.1 mmol/L or above, 1 hour 10.0 mmol/L or above, 2 hour 8.5 mmol/L or above. Initial management is dietary review plus home glucose monitoring 4 times a day. Pharmacotherapy is added when targets are missed after 1 to 2 weeks of lifestyle change.
key_points: ADIPS thresholds: fasting 5.1, 1 hour 10.0, 2 hour 8.5
Single elevated value diagnoses GDM
First-line management: lifestyle plus home monitoring
Pharmacotherapy added if targets missed on lifestyle
explanation.pearls: Postnatal 75 g OGTT is done at 6 to 12 weeks after birth in all women with GDM to identify persistent type 2 diabetes; those women who screen negative postnatally still need lifetime 1 to 3 yearly diabetes screening.

sources.label: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for Gestational Diabetes 2014
RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 7 Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes

subtopic_detail: Suspected uterine rupture during trial of labour
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar covering the birthing suite. A 34 year old G2P1 is having a trial of labour after one previous caesarean at 39 weeks for breech.

She is 6 cm dilated at 4 hours into active labour with a syntocinon augmentation running. Over the last 10 minutes she has developed sudden severe suprapubic pain that is now constant between contractions and has become more distressed. The CTG shows a new prolonged deceleration to 70 beats per minute for 4 minutes. On palpation the presenting part appears to have risen out of the pelvis and the abdomen feels firm and tense. Her BP has fallen to 92/56 from 118/74 at last check 30 minutes ago and she is tachycardic at 128. Her cervix has become oedematous.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128, BP 92/56, RR 22, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.6, FHR 70 for 4 minutes
data_table.Examination: Distressed; abdomen tense; presenting part risen; oedematous cervix
data_table.Investigations: CTG prolonged deceleration to 70; last cervical assessment 6 cm 30 minutes ago
data_table.Medications: Syntocinon augmentation infusion running at 12 mU/min

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate step in management?

options.text: Stop syntocinon, apply left lateral tilt, and reassess CTG for 10 minutes for recovery
options.rationale: Stopping syntocinon and repositioning is appropriate for isolated non-recurrent decelerations without maternal or clinical concern; the constellation of sudden severe pain, risen presenting part, maternal shock, and prolonged deceleration is uterine rupture requiring immediate transfer to theatre (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned VBAC and Trial of Labour After Caesarean).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned VBAC and Trial of Labour After Caesarean

options.text: Perform an artificial rupture of membranes to expedite progress and improve the CTG trace
options.rationale: ARM in the setting of prolonged deceleration and suspected rupture is contraindicated and delays definitive management; the patient needs laparotomy not augmentation (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned VBAC and Trial of Labour After Caesarean).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned VBAC and Trial of Labour After Caesarean

options.text: Administer intravenous terbutaline 250 mcg to relax the uterus while awaiting theatre availability
options.rationale: Tocolysis is used for hypertonic uterine activity causing foetal compromise where rupture is not suspected; in suspected rupture it delays surgical intervention which is the definitive treatment and offers no benefit (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned VBAC and Trial of Labour After Caesarean).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned VBAC and Trial of Labour After Caesarean

options.text: Call emergency and transfer to theatre for immediate category 1 caesarean section delivery
options.rationale: The clinical picture of sudden severe abdominal pain, loss of station, maternal haemodynamic collapse, and prolonged deceleration in a trial of labour after caesarean is classic uterine rupture; immediate category 1 caesarean and laparotomy is the only intervention that can salvage foetal and maternal outcomes (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned VBAC and Trial of Labour After Caesarean).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned VBAC and Trial of Labour After Caesarean

options.text: Insert an intrauterine pressure catheter to quantify contraction strength and diagnose obstruction
options.rationale: An intrauterine pressure catheter has no role in the diagnosis of uterine rupture and delays theatre transfer; suspected rupture is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate laparotomy (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned VBAC and Trial of Labour After Caesarean).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned VBAC and Trial of Labour After Caesarean

explanation.summary: Uterine rupture during VBAC classically presents with sudden severe abdominal pain, loss of station, maternal haemodynamic collapse, and foetal bradycardia. It is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate category 1 caesarean and laparotomy. Tocolysis, ARM, or pressure catheters are contraindicated and delay definitive care.
key_points: Rupture triad: sudden pain, foetal bradycardia, maternal collapse
Loss of station and abdominal tenderness support diagnosis
Category 1 caesarean is the only intervention
Delay in delivery beyond 18 minutes worsens neonatal outcomes
explanation.pearls: The incidence of uterine rupture in TOLAC after one lower segment caesarean is approximately 0.5 to 1 per cent; syntocinon augmentation raises this to about 1.5 per cent and requires careful monitoring.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned VBAC and Trial of Labour After Caesarean
Australian Council on Safety and Quality in Health Care Maternity Standards

subtopic_detail: Postpartum contraception with breastfeeding and VTE history
stem:
You are the GP registrar seeing a 33 year old woman at 6 weeks postpartum for her routine review.

She is fully breastfeeding a healthy 6 week old infant and plans to continue exclusive breastfeeding to 6 months. She had a distal deep vein thrombosis in her right leg during her second trimester managed with therapeutic enoxaparin, transitioned to prophylactic dose at 36 weeks, and continued for 6 weeks postpartum which ceased 2 days ago. Thrombophilia screen was negative. She wants effective contraception starting today, does not want an intrauterine device, and does not smoke. Her BP is normal and BMI is 26.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 72, BP 118/72, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.6
data_table.Examination: No leg swelling; fundus involuted; well healed perineum
data_table.Investigations: Thrombophilia screen negative; last dose enoxaparin 2 days ago
data_table.History: Fully breastfeeding; second trimester DVT; non-smoker; BMI 26

lead_in: What is the most appropriate contraceptive to recommend?

options.text: Combined oral contraceptive pill 30 mcg ethinyloestradiol plus levonorgestrel taken continuously
options.rationale: The combined pill is UKMEC 4 (unacceptable) in the first 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women due to VTE and lactation effects, and past DVT further contraindicates oestrogen containing methods (Source: FSRH UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use; Family Planning Australia Contraceptive Guidelines).
source_refs: FSRH UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

options.text: Vaginal ring releasing etonogestrel plus ethinyloestradiol 15 mcg over 21 days per cycle
options.rationale: The vaginal ring contains oestrogen and shares the contraindications of the combined pill; past VTE plus lactation both contraindicate its use in this patient (Source: FSRH UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use).
source_refs: FSRH UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

options.text: Progestogen only pill (desogestrel 75 mcg) taken at the same time daily starting today
options.rationale: Progestogen only pill is compatible with breastfeeding, safe with a past history of DVT, and can be started immediately in a low risk postpartum woman; desogestrel provides a 12 hour missed pill window and is preferred over the 3 hour levonorgestrel POP (Source: Family Planning Australia Contraceptive Guidelines; Australian Medicines Handbook).
source_refs: Family Planning Australia Contraceptive Guidelines
Australian Medicines Handbook

options.text: Lactational amenorrhoea method alone with review at 6 months when weaning is planned
options.rationale: The lactational amenorrhoea method requires exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea, and the infant to be under 6 months old to be 98 per cent effective; she wants effective contraception and additional coverage is prudent given the constraints (Source: Family Planning Australia Contraceptive Guidelines).
source_refs: Family Planning Australia Contraceptive Guidelines

options.text: Levonorgestrel intrauterine device inserted today in the clinic after informed consent
options.rationale: She has explicitly declined intrauterine methods; the question asks for the most appropriate contraceptive given her preferences and safety profile (Source: Family Planning Australia Contraceptive Guidelines).
source_refs: Family Planning Australia Contraceptive Guidelines

explanation.summary: Combined hormonal contraception is contraindicated by past VTE and by the first 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women. Progestogen only methods are safe in both scenarios. Desogestrel POP has a wider missed pill window (12 h) than levonorgestrel POP (3 h). LAM alone requires strict criteria that a mother returning to work may not meet.
key_points: Combined hormonal methods contraindicated by past VTE
Progestogen only methods safe in breastfeeding and past VTE
Desogestrel POP has 12 hour missed pill window
LAM needs exclusive breastfeeding, amenorrhoea, infant under 6 months
explanation.pearls: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate is another progestogen only option but should be delayed to 6 weeks postpartum in breastfeeding women per Family Planning Australia; POPs can be started earlier.

sources.label: FSRH UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use

subtopic_detail: Antepartum haemorrhage in known placenta praevia
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar receiving a call from the emergency triage nurse. A 30 year old G3P2 at 32+2 weeks with a known low lying anterior placenta (edge 8 mm from internal os on 28 week scan) has arrived by ambulance with painless fresh red vaginal bleeding.

She estimates the loss at two soaked pads and one on arrival that is half saturated. She has no abdominal pain, no uterine contractions, and no ruptured membranes. She has had one prior caesarean birth. Her BP is 108/68, pulse 96. CTG is reassuring with a baseline of 140 and moderate variability. She is Rh negative. Her group and antibody screen from booking is valid. She has not had betamethasone this pregnancy.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 96, BP 108/68, RR 18, SpO2 98% room air, temperature 36.7, FHR 140 reassuring
data_table.Examination: Soft non tender abdomen; no palpable contractions; no visible external bleeding now
data_table.Investigations: 28 week scan low lying anterior placenta 8 mm from internal os; Hb baseline 118 g/L
data_table.History: One prior caesarean; Rh negative; no betamethasone this pregnancy; blood group and antibody screen valid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management sequence?

options.text: Perform a digital vaginal examination now to assess cervical dilatation and rule out preterm labour
options.rationale: Digital vaginal examination in known or suspected placenta praevia risks provoking catastrophic haemorrhage and is contraindicated until praevia has been formally excluded by ultrasound and placenta location confirmed (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum

options.text: Commence syntocinon augmentation to accelerate labour and expedite vaginal birth to control bleeding
options.rationale: Augmenting labour in placenta praevia is dangerous and vaginal birth is contraindicated when the placenta is close to or covering the os; syntocinon has no role here (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum

options.text: Proceed to emergency category 1 caesarean section for maternal and foetal safety immediately
options.rationale: Immediate delivery is indicated for uncontrolled maternal haemorrhage or foetal compromise; a stable mother with reassuring CTG and settling bleeding can be admitted and stabilised with corticosteroid cover for prematurity before decisions about delivery timing (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum

options.text: Discharge home with outpatient ultrasound in 48 hours given the bleeding has visibly slowed
options.rationale: APH at 32 weeks with known low lying placenta always requires inpatient admission because rebleeding can be catastrophic and unpredictable; outpatient management is not appropriate (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum

options.text: Admit for continuous monitoring, administer betamethasone 11.4 mg IM, give anti-D immunoglobulin, cross match blood
options.rationale: APH with known low lying placenta at 32 weeks requires admission for continuous monitoring, antenatal corticosteroid course for preterm lung maturation, anti-D for Rh negative mothers with sensitising events, and cross matching red cells for potential deterioration; digital examination is deferred pending speculum (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum).
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum

explanation.summary: APH with known low lying placenta at 32 weeks requires admission, continuous monitoring, corticosteroid course for preterm lung maturation, anti-D for Rh negative mothers, and cross matching. Digital vaginal examination is contraindicated. Delivery is reserved for uncontrolled bleeding or foetal compromise.
key_points: No digital examination in known or suspected praevia
Corticosteroids for preterm lung maturation if <34 weeks
Anti-D within 72 hours for Rh negative sensitising event
Cross match blood and hold in bank
explanation.pearls: A placenta with edge more than 20 mm from the internal os on third trimester ultrasound is no longer praevia and vaginal birth is generally safe; below 20 mm confers increasing risk of bleeding and often prompts elective caesarean.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 20 Placenta Praevia and Placenta Accreta Spectrum

subtopic_detail: Lithium long-term monitoring schedule
stem:
You are the community psychiatry registrar reviewing a 42 year old man who has been on lithium 900 mg nocte for 6 years for bipolar 1 disorder with excellent mood stability.

He has had no manic or depressive relapses since dose stabilisation 4 years ago. His last routine bloods were 6 months ago and were unremarkable. He describes new fine hand tremor that worsens when he lifts a coffee cup and a 3 kg weight gain over the last 6 months. He denies polyuria, polydipsia, or fatigue. He wants to know what routine monitoring he needs going forward and what should happen if any lab values are abnormal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76, BP 132/82, RR 14, SpO2 99% room air, temperature 36.7
data_table.Examination: Fine hand tremor bilateral; euthyroid on palpation; no oedema
data_table.Investigations: Last routine bloods 6 months ago; eGFR 82, TSH 2.4, calcium 2.34, lithium 0.72 mmol/L
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 900 mg nocte for 6 years

lead_in: What is the most appropriate routine monitoring schedule for this patient?

options.text: 6 monthly lithium level plus annual renal function, TSH, calcium, weight, and blood pressure
options.rationale: Stable patients on lithium have 6 monthly lithium levels and annual renal function, thyroid function, calcium, weight, and blood pressure per RANZCP; frequency increases if a level is out of therapeutic range or symptoms develop (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Clinical Practice Guidelines: Bipolar Disorder).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Clinical Practice Guidelines: Bipolar Disorder

options.text: Annual lithium level with 5 yearly renal, thyroid, calcium, and no other routine assessments
options.rationale: Lithium monitoring intervals are 6 monthly for stable patients not annual; and thyroid, renal, and calcium are 12 monthly not 5 yearly per Australian and international guidance (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Clinical Practice Guidelines: Bipolar Disorder).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Clinical Practice Guidelines: Bipolar Disorder

options.text: Monthly lithium level plus 6 monthly TSH and eGFR while the patient remains asymptomatic
options.rationale: Monthly monitoring is used for dose initiation or after dose change; monthly is not required for stable long term maintenance where 6 monthly is sufficient (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Clinical Practice Guidelines: Bipolar Disorder).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Clinical Practice Guidelines: Bipolar Disorder

options.text: Quarterly ECG plus annual echocardiogram to screen for cumulative cardiovascular toxicity
options.rationale: Routine cardiac imaging is not part of lithium monitoring; ECG is only obtained at initiation and when clinically indicated for arrhythmia (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Clinical Practice Guidelines: Bipolar Disorder).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Clinical Practice Guidelines: Bipolar Disorder

options.text: Annual lithium level with parathyroid hormone testing only when calcium abnormalities are documented
options.rationale: Annual lithium levels are insufficient for stable maintenance; the interval is 6 monthly and calcium screening is annual with PTH added if calcium is elevated (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Clinical Practice Guidelines: Bipolar Disorder).
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Clinical Practice Guidelines: Bipolar Disorder

explanation.summary: Long term lithium monitoring requires 6 monthly lithium levels and annual renal function, TSH, calcium, weight, and blood pressure. Frequency increases at initiation, after dose change, or if levels are out of range. Calcium is checked because of the risk of parathyroid hyperplasia; PTH is added if calcium is high.
key_points: 6 monthly lithium levels for stable patients
Annual renal, thyroid, calcium, weight, BP
PTH added if calcium elevated (parathyroid hyperplasia)
Fine tremor is common but coarse tremor suggests toxicity
explanation.pearls: Lithium levels are drawn 12 hours after the last dose (trough level); a delay of even 1 hour in sampling time significantly changes interpretation.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists Clinical Practice Guidelines: Bipolar Disorder

subtopic_detail: TCA overdose with QRS widening
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar. A 22 year old woman is brought in by ambulance after her flatmate found her drowsy with an empty box of amitriptyline 50 mg tablets beside her bed.

She reports taking 30 tablets 2 hours ago. She is drowsy but responds to voice. Her airway is patent. Vital signs: pulse 128 sinus, BP 96/58, RR 20, SpO2 96%, temperature 36.8. ECG shows sinus tachycardia with QRS 148 ms, R wave in aVR of 5 mm, and a rightward frontal axis. She has cool peripheries and 2 seconds capillary refill. Her serum bicarbonate is 18 and lactate 2.4. Blood glucose is 5.4 and paracetamol level is negative.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 sinus, BP 96/58, RR 20, SpO2 96% room air, temperature 36.8
data_table.Examination: Drowsy responsive to voice; cool peripheries; capillary refill 2 seconds
data_table.Investigations: ECG QRS 148 ms; R in aVR 5 mm; rightward axis; bicarbonate 18; lactate 2.4

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate specific therapy?

options.text: Intravenous flumazenil 200 mcg titrated to reverse the residual sedation and drowsiness
options.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines and has no role in tricyclic toxicity; giving it in mixed overdose may precipitate seizures and unmask cardiotoxicity (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).
source_refs: Australian Poisons Information Centre

options.text: Intravenous physostigmine 2 mg over 5 minutes to reverse the anticholinergic component
options.rationale: Physostigmine is contraindicated in tricyclic overdose because it precipitates asystole and seizures in the setting of sodium channel blockade; anticholinergic features are not the therapeutic target (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).
source_refs: Australian Poisons Information Centre

options.text: Intravenous sodium bicarbonate 8.4 per cent bolus 1 to 2 mmol per kg titrated to QRS narrowing
options.rationale: QRS greater than 100 ms plus haemodynamic compromise and an R wave in aVR greater than 3 mm indicate significant tricyclic sodium channel blockade; hypertonic sodium bicarbonate boluses reverse the blockade by increasing extracellular sodium and correcting acidaemia, titrated to QRS narrowing and pH 7.45 to 7.55 (Source: Australian Resuscitation Council; Australian Poisons Information Centre).
source_refs: Australian Poisons Information Centre

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g bolus to prevent torsades de pointes as prophylaxis
options.rationale: Magnesium is used for torsades from QT prolongation; tricyclic toxicity is primarily sodium channel blockade with QRS widening, and hypertonic bicarbonate is the specific treatment before magnesium is considered (Source: Australian Poisons Information Centre).
source_refs: Australian Poisons Information Centre
